utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for the day, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Tom Hannis, Belinda Pidwell and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. While the witness is being escorted in, there are two matters which the Chamber -- with which the Chamber wishes to deal. The first is that the Trial Chamber is seized of an oral motion first raised by the Stanisic Defence on the 13th of April, seeking sanctions against the Prosecution for alleged failure to disclose material relating to the witness Andrija Bjelosevic pursuant to Rule 66(B) of the Rules. The Trial Chamber notes that it does not have a copy of the request for disclosure made by the Defence on the 21st of January, 2011, nor of the Prosecution's response. The Stanisic Defence is accordingly ordered to file with the Trial Chamber by noon on Monday next a copy of the request of the 21st of January, 2011, together with a reply from the Prosecution and confirmation of date on which any disclosure of the documents was made in response to the request. The second matter is that we have seen the proposed list of witnesses for next week and we note that the witness that the Stanisic team indicates it would call in the gap between the conclusion of the testimony of the witness presently on the stand and the return of Mr. Bjelosevic is such that, for ourselves, we don't understand how arithmetically that witness could be completed within the day, day and a half, that we estimate would be remaining, because we were under the impression that Mr. Bjelosevic was a firm fixture for the Monday following, namely the 16th, and it would be useful if counsel could clarify this for us. Not immediately, but at some point probably early next week as to whether their proposal is that the demographers -- there be a break in the testimony of the demographer or that the fixture in relation to the return of Mr. Bjelosevic be varied to follow the demographer. But counsel would inform us accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, we can do that after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, the -- good morning to you. I remind you, you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Yesterday, I was talking with you near the end of the day about your work at state security in Ilidza in 1992, and I had asked you about whether you had interviewed any non-Serbs during that time. I want to ask you about a particular person and whether you know an individual named Perica Koblar, K-o-b-l-a-r, is the last name, he is Slovenian by ethnicity. Does that name ring any bells for you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe his nickname was Pero, Pero Koblar. Says his wife was a schoolmate of yours. Mr. Koblar apparently was -- although Slovenian, he was living in Sarajevo and when the war broke out he eventually was conscripted into the ABiH army and was captured by Serbian forces in mid-July 1993. And he says he was captured by some men under the command of a Brne Gavrilovic. Do you know who Mr. Gavrilovic was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know who this man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges who he was, what you know about him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much, but I do know that this gentleman at the very beginning of the war was in charge of a small military formation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Some have described him as a sort of self-styled Chetnik Vojvoda who had a group of men, armed men, under his control and he operated in the Sarajevo area, particularly in the Ilidza area. Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are well-known facts about that gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, and you'll have to excuse my pronunciation, was there in Ilidza municipality a substation or a police station in a town or a village or an area called B-l-a - and the first letter is the z, like in Zupljanin - z-u-j. Blazuj. Am I pronouncing that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilidza was a municipality and it consisted of a number of local communities. I don't know exactly how many, but one of them was Blazuj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand there was some sort of military police facility located in Blazuj during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a facility of the military police. There was one of the brigade of the VRS, one of the brigades. But I don't know of any separate facility of the military police. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about the MUP, did the MUP have any sort of facility there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, members of the MUP in the territory of the Ilidza municipality were under the SJB of Ilidza which is the municipal centre. This is about 8 kilometres from Blazuj. The SJB was in the centre, as I said, and the MUP members were located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that then, let me show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we continue with something else, even if it is related, in -- on page 4, line 2, you asked, "Would you disagree with that?" And the answer is "Yes." But I think what the witness meant was something else when we read the following, "These are well-known facts," so perhaps it would be good to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't notice that. I took that as agreement but I will follow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I asked you earlier about whether you would agree with the description of Brne Gavrilovic as a self-styled Chetnik Vojvoda who had a group of armed men serving under him in the Ilidza area. Do you agree that that is an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you with this description that the gentleman with this last name led such a group. Whether he is self-styled leader or anything else is something that was never an object of my interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that group, what would you describe them as, were they part of the MUP, a part of the VRS, or some sort of paramilitary formation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned that I took no private or professional interest in this group ever. I know that they existed as a small military formation and I know that soon all such formations were disbanded pursuant to the orders of the highest leadership and they were put under the command of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that there were orders issued to have that accomplished. But I ask you, in Ilidza did that, in fact, happen? Did Mr. Gavrilovic and his group subordinate themselves to the VRS or did they continue to operate independently, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give an answer from memory, it won't be very detailed. As far as I remember, all formations, or rather, their members, were eventually placed under the control of the VRS. I couldn't give you a date for this group or any other, but that wasn't part of my job. My professional duties were not related to these groups while I was in the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P756. This will be coming up on your screen in a minute. It's a document dated 11 September 1993 from the commander of a reserve police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a tab, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think I have a tab. This is one of the documents from Mr. Nielsen's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely why I raised the issue of the information which was given to us two days ago. Your Honours, we cannot be prepared for all expert Nielsen reports, all sessions of government, all whatever Presidency sessions. They have to be listed and given to us so we can have this. As we have all these other binders, we need to have all these documents in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, my recollection, unfortunately, is weak, but I think that when you were cross-examining the Prosecution's witnesses, we allowed both Defence teams to put documents to witnesses to jog their memories even though those documents hadn't been announced in advance and we did so because we realised that it isn't possible to anticipate everything. So once in a while, if there is a need to show a document to a witness in order to jog that witness's memory, we allowed it and with an added that, of course, that document could not be admitted into evidence because it had not been announced previously. Is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But those were the situation that happened only exceptional -- in exceptional circumstances. Now, the problem here is a different problem. The agreement between the parties during the Office of the Prosecutor case was that we list the document, we announce the document that we are going to use. Now, we received the announcement of the documents and then received an additional mail where it says all the documents from expert Nielsen report, all the documents, all the sessions of the government, all the sessions of Presidency, without specifying them. And that is a problem because the announcement of the document was not specific enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is the Court correct in understanding that you are putting this witness -- this document to the witness in order to jog his memory about a certain event in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and about whether or not there was a police station or a reserve police station at a certain location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed. As Mr. Zecevic says, this is an exceptional situation, but it's probably unavoidable. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just indicate for future reference with regard to Mr. Nielsen, documents in evidence between the numbers of P454 and P872 are documents from Mr. Nielsen's report, so in terms of a range, it's identifiable. If you see me calling for an exhibit number in that range, that will be one that came from Mr. Nielsen's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I really think that this is unacceptable. If we were required all the time during the OTP case to clearly specify the documents, to give the tab numbers and announce them for the cross-examination, I believe that such an obligation must be imposed upon the Prosecutor as well. What Mr. Hannis has just said he announced, I don't know, 800 documents from number so-and-so to number so-and-so, this is clearly unacceptable. We must have the exact numbers and the sequence of the documents to be able to properly prepare for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, your last answer, documents between numbers so-and-so, does that mean that, in your opinion, these documents are on your document list for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my intention. When I notified the Defence that in addition to the list of 84 or 100 that we had, I think -- I wanted to alert them that I might use any document from Christian Nielsen's report and from this witness's report. I could have printed it out and had a separate list of each one and I could still do that, if that helps. But I would say that during the Prosecution's case in-chief, when we got notification from the Defence of exhibits they were going to use, typically, what we got was a list of ERNs, not any description of the document, not a date of a document, just the ERNs. And we regularly, frequently got in the middle of direct examination further list of documents that they might use, which is typical and understandable. It happens as things come up in examination. The remedy, I would say, is not to bar me from using these documents, but if the Defence can specify to you in some way why they were prejudiced or why they need more time to deal with the document, that would be the appropriate remedy, rather than precluding me from showing you something that is relevant and helpful to your job in determining the truth and finding the facts in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not unmindful of the practical difficulty which the opposite side has in situations such as with which we are now concerned, but we are unable to appreciate how, especially respect of documents that are already in evidence, the Prosecution can be required to do other than they have done. And as Judge Harhoff has said, this has been the practice that we have followed up to this point. The remedy, and we adopt what Mr. Hannis has said, is that if there is demonstrated prejudice, then the Defence would be allowed time to put themselves in the position to adequately deal with the document which they were unable to locate. But we are, with respect, unable to see how we could prevent the Prosecution from proceeding in the manner that they are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I want to point out the danger that this practice presents. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of the guide-lines for the announcement of documents, paragraphs 14 and 15: [In English] "Upon the witness making the solemn declaration pursuant to Rule 90, the cross-examination party shall provide electronically to the Trial Chamber, the Registrar, and the other parties a list of the documents and other material they may use in cross-examination." Paragraph 15: "If any party wish to use material which has not been timely noticed pursuant to this guide-line, it may only to do so with the leave of the Trial Chamber." [Interpretation] What does this mean in practice? The way we understand it, documents are announced for all parties to the proceedings to be able to follow and participate. This kind of announcement of documents means that the accused, because it's their primary interest, can only follow documents shown by the Prosecution. They can't see the entire document because they cannot access e-court. Our practice is that we give the accused copies of the documents that we are going to use and the other party as well as the OTP, so as to be able to receive instructions from them, either for cross-examination or examination-in-chief. In this way, the accused are prevented from following the proceedings in the proper way and that will affect the fairness of the trial and the final outcome and that is the primary interest of this court. Technically, such an announcement of Mr. Hannis, he said that he would use 800 documents, without specifically pointing them out, we had no possibility to print them out and give them to the accused because it's about them. Nor can we properly follow the cross-examination. This is the prejudice to the Defence due to such an approach. If -- if the OTP were allowed to proceed this way, then next time they could say they -- we will use documents from the 65 ter list from number 1.000 to number 15.000. That would be the logical consequence. Or I could say next time I am going to use documents from number PX through PY, and this is the danger that originates from this approach both for the Trial Chamber and the parties to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't wish to misunderstand you, Mr. Krgovic, but do I understand your proposition to be that this would mean that even in respect of documents that are already in evidence, the Prosecution cannot be allowed to put them to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course they can, Your Honour, but in a way that enables the Defence to show these documents to the accused because they cannot follow the proceedings or the documents because they can only see what is shown on the screens. They cannot see the entire document and they cannot give us instructions for that reason. They cannot access e-court. Secondly, documents that were admitted through the bar table or through Witness Nielsen possibly there were no questions asked about these documents in the courtroom at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are sorry to have taken your time, but this is a problem that has reoccurred at many occasions during the Prosecution's case and also so far in the Defence case, and we are sure that it is a problem that will occur many times yet in the future. The Chamber's view is that we would require the parties to be as specific as possible when they announce their documents that they are going to use with the witnesses. Having said this, however, the Chamber realises that you can't always get it right because from time to time there will be a need to put a document to a witness that has not been announced in advance. And the Chamber will then take a position from case to case, but we do accept that there is occasionally a document that it would make sense to put to a witness even if that document has not been announced. So the bottom line is that we invite, again, the parties to be reasonable, to be as specific as possible putting, as the Prosecution has done in this case, 800 documents forward in order to be on the safe side is perhaps a bit too extreme. Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Zecevic do have a point in that this is simply not -- it's not possible to overlook and to go over all 800 documents with the accused in advance, yet, on the other hand, to require the Prosecution to be so specific that they can only announce documents that they are sure that they are going to use is also too extreme. That would be too narrow, simply. So our advice is to all three parties, be reasonable, be as specific as you can, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, very short comment. But that is precisely -- we understand, we are -- we have been cross-examining the witnesses as well, we know that there is a situation where you need to have an additional document, and we don't have a problem with that, and the guide-lines say you can -- the party can use document with the leave of the Trial Chamber. That's fair enough. That's no problem. The problem is you cannot say I'm going to use 600 documents and when, in fact, you know that you are going to use -- because in the time that you have you can use only 50 of them, so you can say I'm going to use this 50 and in case -- in case there's something is needed, an additional document is needed, I will approach the Trial Chamber and ask for leave to -- that is precisely the point that we are trying to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That point is well understood and recognised by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I think I did indicate putting forward, as Mr. Hannis has done, 800 documents is too extreme. So in the future, I guess we will try to live with this uncertainty that, from time to time, there will be a need to show documents to a witness unannounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I just have to make one response. It's rather serendipitous that Mr. Zecevic should mention the number 600 because when Christian Nielsen came to testify the initial disclosure we got from the Defence on exhibits they wanted to use on cross-examination was 600. After he had started to testify, we got a second list of additional documents they wanted to use which was about a hundred documents. And then before his final cross-examination was done, we got a second -- a supplemental list of 50 additional documents, and I can assure you they didn't use 750 documents during the cross-examination. I take the point but what is -- what is the harm here? If I gave him a list of 800 documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I suggest we stop here and just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you should have on the screen a document dated 11 September 1993. If we could go to the last page, I want to ask you if you recognise the name of the person who sent this document. Do you know who he was, Dusan Kalajdzic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know who this person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I ask counsel, do the accused see the documents when they are shown to us on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you see he is listed as commander of the Blazuj reserve police station. Does that refresh your recollection about whether or not there was a reserve police station in Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't remind me of that, but as I saw the first page, if the gentleman who is mentioned here as the signatory is the author of the text, then it is a completely uneducated person because the heading on the first page of the document is completely inaccurate. It does not reflect the actual organisation within the ministry. And the text itself is written in a spirit, and I'm talking about the first page, which does not imply official correspondence, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, could we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you point to us the portion which you say indicates this is not official correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the style and I will refer you to one error. There was no police station of public security in Ilidza but just the public security station in Ilidza so this is the first egregious error in the heading itself. And further on, Ilidza public security police station in the normal organisation which was envisaged, something like that never existed, not even with the abbreviations which are used here, the JBRM station Blazuj. And finally, I mention the style.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has an intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would -- I just have a suggestion that Mr. Hannis instructs the witness to slowly speak, otherwise I see that the interpreters are struggling to catch what he is saying and interpret that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bajagic, again we would remind you to slow down. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to continue or add anything further?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something was left out of the record, I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the last part I see recorded in the transcript, you said this abbreviation used here was not appropriate, the JBRM, and you're also recorded as saying, "Finally, I mentioned the style." Is there anything else that you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But beneath that, we see that there is a document number or a registry number. That is typically something that would be included in official MUP correspondence, wouldn't it, the 01-33/93?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a location and a date?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To be the commander of a reserve police station in the RS MUP in 1993, were there any minimal educational requirements, do you know, under the law and the rules?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly were the requirements for somebody to be the commander of reserve police force. I know that to be commander of a police station you had to have had secondary education completed and, if possible, university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I've gotten far afield from where I started out with this. I was trying to establish what police presence there was in Blazuj in Ilidza municipality. Did you -- do you recall ever having gone to Blazuj to do any of your work in connection with the military police located there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the three and a half years during which I worked there, there were countless times that I passed through Blazuj or went there, but to remember exactly something specific is rather difficult after almost 18 or 19 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Koblar, who said he recognised you as a person from Ilidza and having been active in the communist youth organisation, I don't remember the exact title that you gave us yesterday, said that you were present in Blazuj at the location where he had been taken to be interviewed by the military police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Koblar remembers about me was known to the majority of citizens of Sarajevo because I was covered in the media by a representative of the youth organisation or the legal students at the time, but I cannot remember the details which he mentioned about me in connection with Blazuj. I simply seem to have forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. He mentions that during the process you happen to see pictures of his wife who apparently had been a schoolmate of yours and that you asked him about her and his family members, does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad if at the time I asked him about his wife, if she had been my schoolmate, but I really do not remember this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours and counsel, just for the record, I'm looking at a document that's at tab 115 of our list of proposed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He indicates that after the initial interview as he was leaving the room, you stopped him and asked if he recognised you and he apologised for not recognising -- and he says you apologised for not having recognised him sooner, because then he, Mr. Koblar, would have been beaten less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, I don't see what is the basis of Mr. Hannis' questions. He is citing the document, we don't know where the document comes from, what is this document. This is the first time we ever saw this document. It was never shown to us. I mean, we had the situation before about the statements, and there was a fierce battle about it and the objection from the Office of the Prosecutor. And if Mr. Hannis want to ask the questions, he can ask the questions, but he cannot refer to the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we -- if we are going to have a further discussion on this, I would ask that the witness be escorted out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, this -- it's not my present intention to try and introduce this document into evidence. As I have objected to the Defence's attempt to introduce the testimony of Alija Delimustafic from Mr. Mandic's state court proceedings, I don't think it's appropriate to get around Rule 92 and introduce some out of court statement by a non-present witness. But it serves as my good faith basis for asking the questions I'm asking. I have a reason to believe that this witness was present at a time when a non-Serb who was being detained by Serb authorities was being questioned, was being beaten. Part of our argument about this witness is that he is too closely tied to the events on the ground, that he has a bias and a prejudice and a motive that undermines his credibility as an expert witness, and I think I'm entitled to ask him those questions. Now, as I understand it and has been the practice in the last trial I did, I'm entitled to ask that question, but I have to live with his answer. If he says, No, I don't know that man; no, I was never present when that happened; no, nobody was beaten in my presence; no policemen ever beat any witness during my three years in state security service, I have to live with that answer and my only remedy is to perhaps seek leave from the Court in rebuttal to call a witness to address it. But for now, either he agrees or remembers and says, Yes that's true or that part is right or that part is not right, but I'm entitled to ask those questions. I can't put in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I understand Mr. Zecevic's objection, he would not disagree with what you have just said. What the -- what his objection is, as I understand it, is that the -- whereas, obviously as an attorney, you may have informed yourself out of court as to the backgrounds on the basis of which you formulated the question. The -- you can't use that piece of information to put to the witness. I think that is as narrow as the objection is. Mr. Zecevic, did I put my finger on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, there's nothing wrong with the question, it's just that you can't refer to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, I think I understand. My problem is I say, He says in the statement you did thus and so, my question should be, Did you tell him you remember his wife after seeing the pictures, something like that. So I'm not making a specific reference to a document. I agree. I think that's the correct procedure, and I may have phrased my questions poorly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we could have the witness back on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies for that interruption. Professor, did you see Mr. Koblar being taken to give an interview before a Crna television crew?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already noted several times that I do not remember this meeting at all and let alone any facts or details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you during your time in state security service ever see or hear about or hear -- actually hear any of your MUP colleagues abusing non-Serb detainees during interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have such information. I haven't heard. I can only guess but I do not have any information that members of the MUP were behaving in such manner, and it was not my duty to have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, whether it's your duty or not, that's the kind of thing that you might hear about in your job -- in the course of your interviews, did you have occasion to interview Serbs who had previously been in the custody of either the Muslim or Croat forces and had been either released, exchanged or had escaped? Did you interview or debrief any Serb individuals during your time in the state security?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they report that they had been abused during their detention?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the situation. I cannot remember specific examples but I know that some of them spoke about such experiences during their interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And given the circumstances of the war and the inter-ethnic conflict, that's not surprising to you, is it, that that sort of thing would happen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever been contacted by or interviewed by anyone on behalf of the state war crimes prosecutor in Bosnia about events in 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if I understood correctly, you mean the Bosnian prosecutor's office. No, nobody contacted me from that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever produced any written account or given any interview to anyone, any investigators or journalist or politician or supervisors about your conduct or your activities within the MUP from 1992 until you left in December 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That especially applies to the media because what I did in the National Security Service must remain confidential, I must keep it to myself. That's stipulated by the rules of service as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does that mean you can't answer questions I ask you today about what you did in the state security service between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but what I meant to say is the following: When I leave the service I shouldn't speak about these things to the media, and there was no reason for me to speak to politicians or other personalities about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's a good practice in general, Professor. Let me ask you to take a look at Exhibit 65 ter 20054. This is at tab 84. This is dated the 2nd of October, 1992, to the under-secretary of the National Security Service, Mr. Kijac, from a Predrag Ceranic, who at the time, apparently, was chief of the SNB sector in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see a list of employees of Sarajevo SNB with activity codes; number 3, Mladen Bajagic, A 03. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is the significance of that number? How were those numbers assigned? Did it have to do with seniority or ranking within the department, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with one's place in the hierarchy, it is merely the code of the operative worker. Probably it was done this way at the time for a reason, but it has nothing to do with the hierarchy in the National Security Service sector. It was just that each operative worker and other member of the service was assigned a code.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if in other SNB Ilidza documents we see a reference to A 03 in 1992, can we assume that's referring to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That's a logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could next take a look at 65 ter 20071. This is tab 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Professor, this is one also from Predrag Ceranic, dated the 2nd of September, 1992, from Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 6 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think number 51, that's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the VSS after your name refers to what, university education? Do you know what that abbreviation stands for? Maybe you can't see it in the B/C/S version, we have to scroll to the far right side of the document.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these abbreviations stand for one's education and I had a university degree at the time, that is noted by this VSS abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you 65 ter number 20068. This is at tab 104. This is dated the 2nd of December, 1992, and the operative referred to is A 03. That would be you in December -- or -- yes, December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the signature at the bottom, do you recognise who is that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the signature of the chief of the department where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And who was that at the time, is that Mr. Sehovac?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When had he replaced Mr. Ceranic as your boss?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but it must have been in late spring or early summer. I cannot be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about the presence of certain paramilitary formations in Ilidza in 1992. We already talked a little bit about Mr. Gavrilovic, and did you ever see or hear -- or hear about a group referred to as Charlie's group or Charlie's men present or operating in your municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember it very vaguely. I need something -- something specific to jog my memory, but I really can't remember everything from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Arkan's Men and specifically Legija, I think is one of his names, was Milorad Ulemek, who was eventually convicted in Serbia in connection with the assassination of Mr. Djindjic. Were you aware of the presence of Legija in Ilidza in 1992 or any other Arkan's Men?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for a number of days they were present, Ulemek and I don't know how many others, but I don't have detailed information because that coincides with the period when I had to be at Vraca for a few days to give instruction. Upon my return, those people were no longer there and I didn't take an interest in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand you were working on state security side and more focused on the enemy, but were you -- well, strike that. Let me ask you, you mentioned you had gone to Vraca for a few days to give instruction. What kind of instruction and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me who instructed others, but rather more experienced members of the National Security Service through conversation and showing me legal regulations and in other ways taught me how to draft my first Official Notes, what the difference is between an Official Note and other types of documents, and the procedures that were applied before the war and the same service in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So some basic knowledge about the functioning of that service. Because before the war I was not part of the MUP system, I was a student, and dealt more with culture-related issues, the youth radio, and so on, and I knew nothing about policing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We talked about Mr. Gavrilovic and his group. Did you know an individual named Sinisa Milic, who had the nickname Mongo, and was apparently a member of Mr. Gavrilovic's paramilitary group? Ever hear of him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Milic was born in Ilidza and his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather were all born there. He was a young man who belonged to one of the most respected families there and practically everybody knew him. I don't know when exactly, but it was at the beginning of the war that he died, and I really don't know that he was a member of Gavrilovic's unit. Yes, but the man is Sinisa Milic and his nickname was Mongo. This is what I know about him. He belonged to a wealthy and highly-respected family in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not know about him allegedly murdering 22 Muslims in June 1992, about the 12th of June, 1992, apparently prisoners that he was either taking to Vogosca or going to Vogosca to pick up? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that now. I only know that he died in unclear circumstances. That was the rumour, but I don't remember any details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you when he died, I'm asking you about when he allegedly killed 22 Muslim prisoners. Mr. Ceranic, your boss, Mr. Kovac and Mr. Cvijetic at CSB, they knew about it didn't they, and you didn't?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it depends on where the event happened and whose jurisdiction that place is. I can immediately add that there's a rule and a principle that everybody goes about the tasks assigned to him. I mean specific operative tasks. Possibly my colleague was tasked to gather information about that, but I didn't have the right to meddle or ask him about his sources of intelligence. It depends on what your task is at any given moment, even if an event happened and it happened in Vogosca municipality. Possibly the headquarters of the National Security Service was informed about that from the relevant department in that municipality, but I don't know that. It may have been from my department, but it may have been processed by another colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But this wasn't some secret event. Wasn't part of the problem in connection with this mass killing by Mongo the fact that it had taken place in the presence of UNPROFOR personnel? Weren't you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that you have in-depth information. I don't know what to say to you. I cannot remember things that are really absent from my memory. I don't have such information from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And us having talked about it now doesn't bring any of it back to you? It sounds like it would have been one of the big events in Ilidza in 1992, given the prominence of Mongo's family, the witnessing of the event by UNPROFOR personnel, none of that rings a bell or refreshes your memory?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for what reason I may have changed my attitude toward that. I said that I don't remember the specific event and I also gave you an answer with regard to Mr. Koblar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see it's time for our first recess, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered in, two things. First, I would like the record to show that Mr. Cvijetic has joined the Stanisic Defence. And the second thing was about the scheduling Your Honours inquired at the beginning of this morning's session. Your Honours, we anticipate that this witness will finish on Wednesday next week. According to our information that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor, that is the -- in our opinion the reasonable estimate. Therefore, having in mind the fact that we are going to be a bit shorter, well, relatively quite shorter with Professor Pasalic, we anticipate that Professor Pasalic will finish his testimony on Monday the week after, which is the -- which is May 16th, or perhaps the first session on Tuesday. Therefore, the witness who is coming, Mr. Bjelosevic, will be perhaps delayed one day, which I think shouldn't be -- shouldn't create a big problem in scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We were alerted to the suggestive time that you would have take within this witness of 10 hours and tried to divide the four-hour sitting day into 10 hours, that is why we were alerted to the possibility, but I follow how you propose to proceed. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, let's move on and talk about your report now. Do you have a copy of it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know you told Mr. Zecevic that that report is your work and your work alone. Did you type it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did all the work alone and I typed it myself. I can use a computer quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sure you can. When did you start working on your report, approximately, if you remember? Day and month, year.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right when I was commissioned by the Tribunal I started to work on this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall that date?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give me an approximate date, a month and a year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in early 2009, spring maybe, I began collecting material and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you finally complete it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was completed in March this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it was filed here with court maybe a six weeks ago. Did you feel that you had adequate time to review it and make all the corrections you wanted to before you turned it in in March of this year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time I thought that I had had enough time, but as we know, no one book or no one text is ever ideal. Even now when I reread it, I notice some mistakes such as a missing comma or possibly a typo or things of that kind. Nothing is ever flawless.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. I completely understand that. We know that you made two changes, two minor changes during your proofing with Mr. Zecevic last weekend and I think Wednesday when you were testifying in the course of your testimony there was one minor change that I think Mr. Zecevic made with you on the record about Exhibit 1D46. And as you've said now, reading it again, you see some minor changes, but are you generally satisfied with the completed product, that there are not any major errors remaining? Sorry, you'll need to answer out loud for the record.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no major errors. Nothing essential, just the regular ordinary technical mistakes. I'm satisfied with the final version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you tell me when you were first approached about writing this report, what was the initial topic you were given?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial topic at the time was the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic from 1990 until 1993, and that is indeed the title of my expert report. Then there's also the subheading which specifies it additionally and reads: Beginnings, purview, jurisdiction, organisation and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you testified Monday at page 20021, you said that: "The first tentative topic for this report was given to me by the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic." And you went on to say that: "The Defence team provided me with the general topic that I was supposed to investigate." And I guess you are telling me that general topic was RS MUP 1990 to 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the meaning of my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me just that topic, RS MUP 1990 to 1993, is a pretty broad topic because, I mean, what are we talking about? Do we want to know the name of every member, we want to know all their activities? You understand what I'm saying? Was it narrowed down to what you were supposed to talk about in relation to the MUP during those three years?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the general topic which was assigned to me, I also received just some suggestions about what some of the topics within the framework should be important and should be developed, but certainly not in such detail as can be found in the report which I submitted. The detailed contents of the report are the result of my methodological approach, which I believe to be necessary in order to be able to take into account what we are discussing here, that is to say, the MUP of the Serbian republic, its beginnings, its establishment, organisation, purview, jurisdiction, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you received some suggestions about what some of the topics should be. From whom did you receive those suggestions, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received these suggestions from the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Specifically, was that Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Cvijetic or both or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said that you received some relevant documents on the basis of which you were to write the report. Can you tell us precisely which documents you received and how many when you began your work on this project, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received a number of legal regulations and other documents, but I cannot remember the exact number, nor did I keep that sort of record while working on my report. And I already had some documents in my possession, specifically the law library as I already had produced another report for this Tribunal in another case which was previous to this engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any rough idea on how many documents? Did you receive hundreds, thousands?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several hundreds of documents which I received from the Defence team. But in dealing with this subject, I came to a significant number of documents through my own research, and I integrated those into the report. Even then, I made some selection so that I would not burden the report with too many footnotes. For certain incidents, I could have mentioned as many as 30 documents in one footnote, but I tried to use just several as references. I classified the documents, and in this way I decided which ones I would include in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of, what, almost two years from starting the project until the completion, did you receive from the Defence additional documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened on several occasions but the number of these documents was very limited. It was a small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember anything particular about the nature of those additional documents you received?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a situation in which I received another legal regulation from the time when the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still operational. Now, whether this was a legal regulation from 1977 which we referred to yesterday or another one from 1990, this is something I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 20022 on Monday, you mentioned that in addition to the documents that were provided to you, you did searches on your own and tried to find documents to help you in writing your report. And in doing so, you found many studies and monographs that you referred to and that are listed in the footnotes. Those studies and monographs referred to in your footnotes, are those all materials you found on your own or were any of those provided to you by the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found on my own all these studies and monographs. In my electronic library I have more than 4.000 documents in pdf format, that includes studies and monograph, I also have several hundreds of such studies in hard copy. So this was exclusively my own material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note in some -- or one of the early sections of your report you have references to a number of books and articles, some which appear to be posted on websites or blogs. Are those postings on websites and blogs included in your term "monograph"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A monograph is a monograph regardless of whether I bought it in a book-shop or ordered it from the publisher or found it through the Gigapedia system, the full text and download it. I have some of such monographs in pdf format and other formats, I have really a number of such monographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm embarrassed to show my ignorance but it's been a long time since I was in an academic setting. When you say monograph, can you tell me what you are referring to? What is your definition?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definition of a monograph is an original academic study done by one person about a specific problem from a certain scientific discipline which has to satisfy certain criteria. It has to have three reviewers who hold the highest academic titles and who would give a positive opinion about the work, and with this in mind it would be categorised within the system that is used to categorise scientific and academic research works.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, that's helpful. When including any of these sources, books or monographs or any of the other sources that are listed in your footnotes, did you -- did you personally vet them; that is, check them out to satisfy yourself that it was a reliable source to depend on in writing your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to note that I'm also a professor who teaches, inter alia, a subject called terrorism and political violence at master studies level. For this subject, I really have lots of research materials. These are all acknowledged authors and I used some of these sources produced by these authors when I was writing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So -- were you finished?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I will add this: I made special effort to use monographs which are used by others, most generally speaking in Europe and worldwide, when dealing with certain specific issues, so these are mostly foreign authors who are researching or discussing certain social phenomena and processes. From the Serbian point of view, they are foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were -- you answered Mr. Zecevic's question at page 20023 on Monday that you had received a copy of Dr. Christian Nielsen's expert report submitted in this case by the Prosecution. And I note that in your own report you have a few footnotes where you make reference to Dr. Nielsen's report, but, as I recall, those footnotes reference his 2004 report which was prepared for the Krajisnik case. Did you not also have a copy of his, basically, updated report from Krajisnik that was prepared in 2008 specifically for this case? Did you have that report as well?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer with full precision on questions relating to Mr. Nielsen's report, not anymore. While I was working on my first report for this Tribunal, I also had one or two versions of Mr. Nielsen's report. But for my report, I believe that I used the version which relates to this case, even if there is an error somewhere, it's an error because I had something else in my memory while I was typing, but I think that it was unimportant. So I have a number of Professor Nielsen's reports with me in electronic versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you would agree that it would probably be important to refer to the report he wrote specifically for this case. And I take it from your answer that you did read his 2008 report as well as the 2004 Krajisnik report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And actually when Dr. Nielsen testified, as I remember, I think that was the first time I saw you, you actually sat in court for part of his testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this happened on several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mention in -- I'll have some further questions about sources later on when we get to specific sections of your report, but now let me ask a few general questions. In your discussion with Mr. Zecevic on Monday, you stated that the Ministry of the Interior is a part of the state authorities in the executive branch of the government. That's correct, isn't it, MUP is part of the executive branch?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Bosnia and the Republika Srpska what other branches do you have? For my jurisdiction I'm familiar with an executive branch, a legislative branch, and a judicial branch, is it the same for you or something different?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is like that in all modern states. The three main branches of authority are the legislative branch, the executive, and the judicial branch. And it was like that in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where would the army fit in? Is the army part of the executive branch of the RS?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence and the armed forces, specifically the Army of Republika Srpska, belonged to the branch of executive power.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. My English dictionary says executive means "having power to carry out decisions and laws, decrees," et cetera. Would you agree with that general definition?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is general and it applies to all those who belong to the executive system, and then by areas they are specified to certain departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason that I am persuing this is that later on in your report, you, on several occasions, refer to the MUP and administrative actions. Maybe it's a question of translation or semantics, but aren't the acts of the MUP members executive actions? Why do you refer to them as administrative actions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you deal with a research pertaining to national police systems and the Ministries of Internal Affairs comparatively anywhere in the world, you can read about several approaches to the notions of what these administrative actions or authorities are. There is a whole branch of researching police functions which calls this authority administrative actions and categorises them as two kinds, administrative actions addressed to items and others which are focused on persons. The Law on State Administration in a legal system of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was like that previously as well, defines the Ministry of the Interior as an organ of state administration. It is the same with the Law on Ministries and if we call something legally a state administration organ, considering what I said and in theory of studying police organisation, what I mentioned can be called administrative actions. Administrative actions or authorities are one in the same thing here. It just depends which terms you would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The reason that I ask is, for me, in English have different connotations for me, and administrative I am more familiar with in a context of something is -- when I started working as a young lawyer I had a secretary, but in later years it became more politically correct to refer to that person as an administrative assistant instead of a secretary. And I think it was yesterday you were talking about situations where the police sometimes have to use force, either firing a fire-arm or using a truncheon to carry out their duties. And, as I recall, you talked about -- that was an administrative action, is that correct, policeman firing his gun or using a truncheon to hit a demonstrator over the head? Is that an administrative action?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a power or authority of the police. As I said, it can be administrative action which is directed to persons or directed to objects. This is just a matter of terminology, so we can agree, you and me, that we are talking about this and then just use the term power or authority. It's not a problem if you don't like this phrase administrative actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate that. I just want to understand it. For me, in my language, it would come as a small consolation to the person arrested and shot or hit over in the head in the course of an arrest being told, Don't worry, it was only an administrative action of a policemen when he did that to you. That's the reason I was trying to understand your use of the term. Now, did you get any instruction or input from the Defence in connection with what you talked about broadening the context? At page 20024 from Monday, you said that as you began working on your report, you realised it was impossible to do the research about its organisation, mission, and so on, unless you put it in a broader context. Did the Defence team give you input on what the broader context should include?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was my assessment. It was impossible to deal with the beginning and foundation of the Ministry of the Interior Serbian republic unless we could see what it was created from and in which social and political circumstances. I believe, generally speaking, it is impossible to single out from reality one institution such as the Ministry of the Interior and see it outside of the actual context in which it was created and developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sounds reasonable to me. You, in your report, in your first section about constituting the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and establishment of organs of state authority, have four subsections. In the first one is the general characteristics of the crisis, which in my English version runs about four pages. Then you have three sections devoted separately to the activities of the SDA and the Muslims, the HDZ and the Croatians, and the SDS and the Serbs. And I think Judge Delvoie commented on this. In English, my -- by my count there are 18 and a half pages devoted to the SDA and the Muslims, 11 pages to the HDZ and the Croats, and 2 and a half pages to the Serbs and the SDS. Is that proportion in your report reflective of your own personal view or opinion about the relative percentage of responsibility each of those three groups should be attributed for the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this has absolutely nothing to do with that. It is not up to me to assess any sort of responsibility. I said that I devoted a certain number of pages to the activities of Muslim members of the SDA, and the HDZ, and the activities of the SDS relating to foundation Republika Srpska were at least interesting to me because I did not want to point to any one in this Tribunal, to anything that is well-known. And I also took into account the fact that while analysing the work of the ministry, I would specifically deal with these activities in my further work. And in each of the activities of each of the three sides in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina one could write up to 15.000 pages rather than 18, 11 and 4 so there is no gradation there. That was not what I was tasked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is it reflective of the relative percentages of the documents that you had received from the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be significant only in part, but the materials which I found on my own, as I said, directed me, for reasons which I mentioned, to work in the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Professor. At page 20025, you talk about the following chapter in your report, the one called the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of BiH in the period from April to December 1992 and you mention that this is the basic chapter where you describe the de jure aspect of the ministry, but you go on to note and say, "Of course, we also had to deal with" -- and please listen carefully and correct me if this is not a correct translation of what you said: "We also had to deal with the -- with the surreal situation and the organisation of the ministry in 1992." Did you mean to say "surreal" or "real"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly real and not surreal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I assumed that's what you intended, although I can see an argument for saying that it was also surreal in some ways in Bosnia in 1992. So the de facto situation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I dealt with the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's dissolution and the creation of the MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are concrete things after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you clearly recognise that there is, as I think Judge Harhoff explored with you -- that there is a de facto situation on the ground which may not always be in line with the de jure situation or order intended. Now, I would agree that looking at the constitution and the laws is a good way to help us understand what the de jure situation was, but what did you look at to help you understand what the de facto situation was in connection with the RS MUP in 1992? Was it only documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also analysed documents, but not only documents, also other materials. Whatever I wrote in a paragraph, I tried to corroborate with a source that refers to the same matter. And it was the sources that determined how deeply I could delve into a problem or how broad my approach should be. I basically dealt with documents of different kinds and it's the facts from these documents that directed my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the beginning of your answer you said you analysed documents but not only documents, also other materials. Can you tell us what kinds of other materials you reviewed or analysed that were not documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, a great many monographs, books written by the immediate participants of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that were published in the past 10 or 15 years, and any other sources I considered potentially useful for drafting my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it that you personally didn't interview anyone, for example?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is sufficient for me if somebody publishes a book, and if that person was a significant participant in the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, then I would use the allegations put forward in that book. I didn't speak to anybody in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us which one of the books you used as a source was written by a person who was a "significant participant in the events"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, Sefer Halilovic's book, "A Cunning Strategy."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I knew you were going to mention him. How about any participant from the Serb side in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the political and military establishment of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are many high officials who wrote memoirs or recollections or similar books. As for persons who were on the Republika Srpska side, I haven't seen anything that they wrote that would be nearly as important to me as Halilovic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you read any trial judgements from the ICTY or Bosnian state court proceedings related to cases arising out of the events in Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visit the official site of this Tribunal very often just to be up to date at a general level. I read the general information, briefs, but I haven't read an entire judgement of this Tribunal or any other court because I didn't consider them interesting. I only took into consideration the information that is the result of a judgement but I haven't read entire judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 20027 on Monday, you were talking about your chapter on the internal organisation of the MUP and the legal framework in particular. You say: "It is necessary, always considering the constitution as the highest legal document of a country, also presenting a number of other pieces of legislation." And then you went on to say you were specifically referring to the Law on the Government, Law on Public Administration, Law on Ministries, and the Law on the Interior. Now, in connection with the law, I note that when you testified as an expert in the Popovic case on October 9th, 2009, at transcript page 26889, you said at line 23: "I'm not a lawyer by profession and I'm not competent to study any details that have to do with criminal law or any other body of law for that matter. I can only share with you what I know about certain provisions on disciplinary measures in the Law on Internal Affairs. However, I do not dare delve any deeper than that since I believe I'm not sufficiently competent." That was in October 2009, do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you had any legal training since October 2009?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even today I don't know the first thing about criminal law and I make no secret of it, but that doesn't mean that I cannot make a quantitative or qualitative analysis of the contents of a text, and that is what I did when I analysed or dealt with the laws and regulations from the Serb Republic of BH. I believe that my academic training and position gives me the right to compare documents, whereas criminal law certainly is a separate professional and line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the quote I read you from Popovic, you were not demurring simply about criminal law, but you said any other body of law apparently outside of certain provisions of disciplinary measures in the Law on Internal Affairs. You are not an expert on constitutional law; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't deal exclusively with constitutional issues here or in my report, I don't go into any detail with regard to that. I only establish a link between constitutional matters and my line of work or the area analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, I have to insist on an answer to my question. You are not an expert on constitutional law; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Nor on statutory construction; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. In order to write a law, you need a team of experts, lawyers and any other professionals who can provide significant assistance depending on the subject matter regulated. It isn't exclusively lawyers that write matters, but also professionals from other areas concerned by this law. A law is always the result of team-work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So do you then consider yourself an expert on statutory construction, and if so, what statutes in particular?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly could be a member of an extended team for making draft laws or even bills, but I'll limit myself to the area of the humanities. Certainly I couldn't say anything about telecommunication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Apart from the report you wrote in this case and your Popovic report, have you ever written about legal interpretation of constitutions of the Republika Srpska or the former Bosnia or any of these various laws? Are those the only two places you've done that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, it was recorded, "I'll limit myself to the area of humanities." It's 44; 9/10. Page 44, line 9 and 10. I don't think that -- either it's not properly recorded. I don't recall hearing anything about it from the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll raise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you heard what Mr. Zecevic just said. Can you help us out with that? Did you say that you were going to limit yourself to the area of humanities or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to social sciences or humanities, if you will. I think that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll repeat my question. Apart from your Popovic report and the report you wrote for this case, have you ever elsewhere written anything about the legal interpretation of constitutions or the various laws that you address in this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly in this way, but in three or four of my monographs, I studied the intelligence and security system of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the time of the socialist republic and after that, and certainly if you analyse the structure of the national security system of a country, you must also analyse the legal framework for several reasons. You must know who adopts laws, the organisation of the work of such service, how they are funded, what kind of control of legality -- of the legality of these services is in place and so on. In my monograph "Espionage in the 21st Century," then in contemporary intelligence and security systems in two editions, one from 2008, the other from 2010, I also deal with the laws and regulations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federation of BH, and the Serb republic, to some extent. Likewise, in the monograph mentioned in my CV, which also has two editions and the title of which is the "Security of the World: From Secrecy to the Public," I also deal with the same matters as in the first monograph. Then in the framework of my institution at the specialist studies level, I teach a subject called security systems. All this boils down to the following: That you cannot speak or deal with the security and intelligence systems of some entities without knowing the legal framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.
