At page 20028, you were mentioning that the Law on the Interior defines the mission and the vision of the MUP and the scope of its work, but you pointed out the law only deals with organisation at a general level, and that it's the rule book that goes into the details. And we've looked at the January 29th, 1990, rule book for the SRBiH that was in effect in the early part of 1992 for the RS MUP, but you also told us that the 1977 rule book about public security operations was something that was also in effect. I want to ask you: Was there no rule book specifically for your side of the house in the MUP, by that I mean state or national security? Did it have a separate rule book for its operations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's not cited in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I don't have that rule book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it not available? Is it a state secret?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had the chance to see that rule book once in my life, and it was the old one of the state security service of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because at the beginning of the war, the National Security Service of the Serb Republic of BH did not have a rule book, so that when I was first briefed about the service, they showed me this rule book, so I -- and I leafed through it once. But its current practice in these services that you can get a rule book to read it and return it upon reading, not everybody could have it on them to keep in a drawer of their desk. Such rule books are official secrets or state secrets and that is the practice throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the RS MUP ever adopt its own rules for state security operations during time you worked there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see a copy of those rules?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones who ran my organisational unit thought that the instructions I had received as an intern was sufficient. Because even if I had had a chance to compare these rule books, then apart from some minor terminological differences, it would have been the same as the previous one, so they didn't consider it necessary to give it to me, but I'd like to have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But having never seen the new rule book, you have no way of knowing whether it's different from the old one, do you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't at all important to me as an operative worker. These rule books are more important for the organisation, the management. It was the most important thing for me to learn what my tasks and duties were, to learn the skills required for intelligence work, and act in accordance with the law. That was important to me as an operative worker and that's the very basic level of personnel, and not dealing with laws and regulations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, at page 20028, you were asked about the annexes to your report, and as I recall, you have 12 separate annexes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 12 is the one that talks about the issue of subordination or re-subordination. Is it correct that the others, the first 11, are separate documents, whereas annex 12 is really more of a supplemental report on the issue of subordination; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when explaining about these annexes, you said: "I came across some documents I considered extremely important for the understanding of both the Ministry of the Interior and the general context into which it came into being." And then you said: "So as not to overburden the report with footnotes, I considered it much more effective to enclose some documents in the report itself." Now, I am afraid, Professor, I don't understand that. How does including 11 of these documents themselves not overburden the report with footnotes which already before we come to the annexes has some 480 footnotes? Can you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inclusion of annexes has nothing to do with the number of footnotes, but rather with the fact that it would be difficult to edit the main part of the text of the expert report. That's why I considered it to be a better solution from the technical point of view to include the annexes at the end and refer to them in the footnotes. This is merely -- this merely has to do with the technical approach, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I was reading your answer and I didn't quite follow. It seems to me that you selected these 11 documents because you thought they were particularly important and you wanted to be sure the Judges saw those actual documents in their entirety; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I opted for the annexes in their present form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We shall reconvene in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, we were talking about your annexes. The -- apart from Annex 12 which you've explained, the other 11 documents that you chose to put in annexes, were those documents furnished to you by the Defence or were those ones you found all on your own or is there some combination?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are mostly documents which I found on my own, some of them are in the law library and I just typed them up and included them in this form in the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. With regard to Annex 12, you testified on Monday that this was created as a result of the Defence's wish from earlier this year about the task of the army and the police during the state of imminent threat of war. Do you remember when you were asked to include this annex, was that in 2011?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in February 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall who on the Defence team requested you to include that or provide that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that request oral or written? I mean, did you get a letter or an e-mail, or did he just ask you orally?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic mentioned it first when he asked me to do that by way of an annex on the telephone. We did not correspond on this or exchange any written notes. We also had a conversation in Belgrade where he mentioned this once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with that were you provided any documents related to what ended up being your Annex 12? From the Defence, I mean, were you provided any documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received documents for the first time from the Defence, I already had one document which is integrated into the annex. Then another integrated document is the Law on All People's Defence which is an open source, you can find it anywhere in Belgrade and in Serbia, and on my own I found in a collection of international documents the protocol and Geneva Conventions which are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it then Mr. Zecevic or nobody from the Defence team provided you any specific new documents in February related to the creation of Annex 12; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Professor, for this next section I'm referring to your testimony on Monday at pages 20029 through -030, and as I did earlier when we talked about monographs, I'm afraid I have to display a little bit of, perhaps, my own ignorance. You said: "The methodology of researching social matters, or the research methodologies in the humanities is unique in the entire world. There's a single methodology." I'm not sure I understand that. Do you mean there's only one way of conducting research in the humanities? Is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As social sciences as a whole cover a very wide area, there is something which is a general methodology of researching social phenomena as a part of the social sciences. It can be specific for sociology or psychology or political science or law, the manner in which it is applied in these areas, but the set of general methods and techniques is almost the same for all social sciences. Therefore, the scientific apparatus which is used to reach certain knowledge when researching a phenomenon is very similar if not quite identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I am sorry, I have to backtrack for a moment, I was reminded that I forgot to ask a couple of questions on the general topic of your assignment to write this report. We talked about specifically in connection with Annex 12, but did you get any written instructions from the Defence team about the preparation of the report, either at the very beginning or during the course of the almost two years that you worked on it? Did you ever receive any written instructions?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The contact was usually verbal, personal, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during those verbal personal contacts, did you sometimes get instructions from the Defence or was it just general discussions about how it was going?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only discussed general issues rather than any specific points or details because when one is conducting this kind of research, he has to be autonomous. The Defence team did not know until the moment when I completed the report what were all the sources which I included, because, as I said, there was a lot of research that I did on my own and that I included as sources in the footnotes so that any going into details or providing me with instructions would violate the methodological concept which I defined for myself as pertaining to the research task which I was given. And considering the classification of the documents for the research, I made a draft or a thesis of my idea. Because, for me, writing this expert report was just the same as doing scientific research which has to be in every aspect founded on relevant sources and has to observe the relevant methodological procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And related to that, did you actually come up with any draft report or draft reports before your final product was done?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not final draft versions. Every evening when I finished my work I would have one draft version. The next day when I started working or seven days later, the draft would sustain certain changes, right, so I never stopped and had one draft version and then continued working on it after a month or two. The report came into being during two whole years, and in addition to writing it, I was also doing other things from the remit of my professional work, that is to say scientific work. I was always going back to the report and as I worked on it, the version kept changing. I did not, however, make some specific draft versions that would be almost final or final, it was only in the end that the report got its shape as it is now. While working on the report, I was also changing the structure of the report depending on the direction that my research was taking at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while you had this work in progress, at any stage did you share the current draft or work in progress with the Defence or were they able to see it and give you any comment or input about that work in progress?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we had occasions to exchange information about the progress of the writing of the report, which stage I had reached or so on, but there were no objections, not in any sense that would have a substantial impact on either the structure of my work or the conclusions that I reached. I would not allow this to anyone, just as I do not allow it when I'm doing my research in general, that anyone should influence my views and positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, that's what I wanted to know. Now, going back to the single methodology that you've talked about using, again transcript page 20030, you said: "If you do research into such an institution," and I think you are referring to the MUP, "or such a process which is a political and legal phenomena and because of that I had to adhere to very strict methodological rules from the very beginning. The first task was the classification of sources by their subject matter, their nature, their contents, and it was necessary to device a codex of classification into various sets." Can you explain to me exactly what is a codex in this context?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you are drafting a research idea whether you want to submit a draft thesis of your masters or PhD thesis, one of its integral parts has to be precisely this codex, this is a matrix on the basis of which you classify documents. In view of your opinion of them, whether they are primary or secondary or tertiary sources, whether they deal with this or that subject. In principle, it is just a framework which you use to help yourself and you indicate to those who are to judge whether your thesis is good or not that you properly classified documents depending on the degree of their importance and taking into account the subject you will deal with and that the thesis refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you still have the codex you prepared for use when making this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I made that, it's in Belgrade. But considering the fact that today we use information technology and we have various abilities, a codex can generally be one folder and within the folder, you can have many sub-folders which you enumerate 1, 2, and 3 and so on. So in one you have the primary documents, and then under folder two you have secondary documents, then tertiary, and in folder number 4 you can just call them other documents. And then you draw on this document as you need them while writing certain sections of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the context of your report about the RS MUP, can you tell me generally what or which documents you considered to be primary documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary documents are all legal regulations which were used to write the report, as well as some other documents relating to the ministry or originating from the ministry and which I found to be very important, and I classified them as such because of their degree of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. From that it sounds like primary doesn't necessarily relate simply to the source, but it also relates to your qualitative impression of those documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And secondary sources, what are those?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, secondary sources are always the sources which indirectly indicate a certain phenomenon, process and so on and so forth. They are not directly related to the subject but they indirectly refer to the subject of research.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tertiary?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tertiary documents can be all other sources that may include the media, various interviews, and other documents which may in some way reflect one of the issues that one is researching, if we judge them to be less important than the other ones. Of course, the documents which I mentioned include scientific works such as monographs and so on, they are always classified as primary or secondary documents. The tertiary ones are those that can sometimes help us to have a wider, fuller and deeper picture of the problem that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a hypothetical question. In the context of this case, how would you classify an interview with Mr. Mico Stanisic about the RS MUP in 1992? Would that be a primary document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what interview you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually I have in mind the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, suspect interview with Mr. Stanisic. Were you aware of that interview?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree that that type of information would be helpful to you when writing your report about the RS MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly find it interesting to read and then on the basis of qualitative analysis of contents, I would hypothetically classify such a document. In any case, this document never came to my hands because it was considered not to be important for the writing of this report and I could not get it in any other way, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do I understand then that if you had known it had existed, you would have liked to have used it in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that I cannot give answers to hypothetical questions. I think that considering all the documents which I received or collected, it was my personal choice which I would select and include in the report which I have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. I don't think you answered my question, Professor, and certainly a professor, you are used to dealing with hypothetical questions, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic was the minister of the RS MUP in 1992, and if you had access to an interview where he was asked questions about the events of 1992, about the creation of the MUP, about the structure of the MUP, about the personnel of the MUP and he was shown documents including many of the documents that you have seen and used in your report and they are used in Christian Nielsen's report, that certainly would be at least something you would want to read before finalising your report; agreed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would gladly have read it, and if I had had this occasion considering your explanation which was quite detailed, it would certainly be classified as one of the documents very important for my report, but that is just hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to your methodology. You said the first step was classification of sources, but then in your answer it is not clear to me what the next step is or how many steps there are in the process. Can you tell us how many steps there are in this single methodology of research in the humanities and what the second and subsequent steps are?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What a thesis of a research work has it to include is the problem which is to be researched, previous knowledge about this subject and problem, the subject of the research, the social and scientific justification, then time and space that are to be covered by the research have to be limited, the hypothetical framework, and a draft structure of the contents. Finally, it should have and it had a list of original sources and documents which would be used but which is then expanded and some of the sources which you already have are, to a certain extent, already classified. And on the basis of all this, you set out and begin the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Part of your answer on Monday was at line 16, page 20030: "In principle, this expert report is the result of a scholarly process. I define hypothesis, I define indicators as material indicators of what could be found in the de facto and de jure sets of the individual problems dealt with, and, of course, the well-known logical processes such as proving, disproving, et cetera." I have a vague recollection of high school or college about the scientific method. Let me ask you: What science are you talking about here, this is social science; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for me social sciences is one that I put in the class of soft science in contrast to what I would call a hard science like physics or chemistry or mathematics, would you agree with that distinction?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There is the group of humanities, technical sciences, and natural sciences. This is a natural division of science in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's not like trying to look at finger-prints or do DNA or ballistics or tool-marks in criminal forensic work where I can basically ask a question and get a firm answer - yes or no - would you agree with me so far?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the context of the research that you were asked to do here, the degree of reliability that you could attach to any conclusions you reach is dependent in part, isn't it, on the amount of relevant material you had to work with? Do you understand that question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to some extent, but what social sciences or political sciences or legal sciences study are things that were created by man and you can never pronounce absolute and final judgements on these things, only with some degree of certainty can you arrive at certain conclusions. Of course you can say about some things that they are hard facts, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry to interrupt. It is just that the first part of the answer was not recorded because the witness was, as usual, hurrying for whatever reason, and so the witness should repeat the second part of his answer so that the rest can be understandable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understood. You are asking him to repeat the first part of his answer or the second part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I am sorry, the second line of his first part of the answer. The first sentence was -- the second part of the first sentence of his answer was not recorded at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, maybe the easiest way to do this would be to just start over, and if you need me to repeat the question, I can do that, or if you have it in mind, just start your answer again and slowly so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat the question because we are discussing complex issues and I can't remember every question, so if you could please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fair. I have to look at the transcript to remember my question. And the question was: In the context of the research that you were asked to do here, the degree of reliability that you could attach to any conclusions you reach is dependent in part, isn't it, on the amount of relevant material you had to work with?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even then I answered in the affirmative and I added an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you add the explanation again because that's where we had a problem with the translation before, and please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to natural science and technology, social sciences study not only man-made things but also processes, events, appearances and phenomena that are in progress or that have some duration. They are never given with certainty. That is why the research into these things is something very complex and you can never reach conclusions that are 100 per cent final. Therefore, in social sciences we speak about scientific forecasts with regard to one set of conclusions as one of the important scientific achievements of the scholar in this area. For example, doctoral theses in this area must hint at a grain of new scientific insight or knowledge which can be expressed through what has been confirmed as a hypothetical framework and a scientific forecast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor, thank you. In some ways I think you and I would approach this matter in a similar fashion. Me as a Prosecutor in the context of this case, my ideal situation would be if I could have all the documents from the RS MUP, every document ever signed or received by Mico Stanisic and all the members of the collegium from, you know, 01-1-92 to the end and every communications log-book and all those same things for every CSB and every SJB, and interviews of every member of all the high-ranking positions. As much information as possible. And I think you, too, would want, in an ideal world, to have access to all that in order to try and reach a conclusion that you could feel most comfortable with. You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but then perhaps there would be no challenge. I'm speaking from the point of view of science, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that your line of questioning here goes to the credibility of the witness and the quality of his report, but since you are not yourself, admittedly, an expert in social science, it might perhaps be worthwhile considering to speed it up and make your point, go directly to the challenge that you wish to push to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, actually the next question I had has a reference to your name and a question that you asked, so I'll try and go to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 20333 on Monday, Judge Harhoff asked you: "What was the common denominator that you would base your conclusions on?" And you said: "I arrived at this common denominator or a general conclusion at the very end of my research. I could only work with a general hypothesis and that is that the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH truly operated in a very difficult period." And then you go on to say: "That is probably a global conclusion that anyone can arrive at, anyone who reads this report." Did you have more specific conclusions based on your research?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other day I also said answering a question that this is one possible general conclusion, whereas all other conclusions I made I offered in the respective paragraphs. It would have been easier for me to speak about individual conclusions I made or some positions of mine in this manner rather than in remembering them. I believe it is not necessary for me to try to remember. It would also be easier for me if I was given a reference to a particular paragraph in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor, I will come to some of those as we go through your report. But with the Court's indulgence, I would like to just ask you a few more questions about what material you used or did not use in preparing your report. Did you, Professor, see the RS MUP annual report covering the period of 1992, because I don't believe it's referenced in your report, and you may recall Dr. Nielsen discussed it at some length in his report? Did you have access to that document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there is no such report that would encompass the whole year for the MUP of the Serb republic of BiH, the time bracket could be from April until the end of the year. I did see that report but I couldn't say exactly when and I don't want to speak from memory. But I know that there's a report from the period from April until December of 1992 for the MUP of the Serb Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one I'm talking about that covers the period from April until December 1992, and I understand your answer to be that you did see that report but you did not find it worthy of mention in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, that's Exhibit P625 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I don't know if you heard my question. So you did read that report, yes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot say now which documents I used from the overall material. That's what footnotes are for. I know that there is a report that spans the period from April to December, but, of course, I cannot say right here and now everything that I cite in my footnotes. Whatever I considered important is mentioned in my footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I know this exhibit is listed, I think, in the list of documents the Defence proposed to use with you at tab 70, but I don't recall seeing it in a footnote in your report, and in the list of documents there's no cross-reference to a footnote. So I take it then you found nothing of sufficient information in that report -- nothing of sufficient importance in that report to note in your report; correct? That's why it's not in a footnote or mentioned in a text anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness already answered that question: "Whatever I considered important is mentioned in my footnotes." 63, 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I will accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about any of the quarterly or annual reports for the CSBs or SJBs, did you have access to any of those, Professor, for various RS MUP organisations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the material that I received there was a report of a CSB, I'm not sure about SJBs, but I repeat, it would be best if you showed me the document and then I could tell you yes or no or find it in a footnote. I find it very difficult to speak from memory. I know that I read some such reports, but remembering a specific situation would amount to speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, we know you looked at Dr. Nielsen's reports. Did you look at any other Prosecution expert reports in this case? For example, specifically, let me ask you some one by one. Did you read Dorothea Hansen's expert report on Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Did you read Ewan Brown's report on the VRS and the military?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assist you, apart from Mr. Nielsen's report, I haven't read any other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that assistance. All right. At page 20035 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 20035 on Monday, you said: "If we take a look at the title of chapter 1 and the four subsections ... one can immediately see that my intention was that I wanted to speak in great detail about the Serbian Ministry of the Interior ... and that for that purpose I had to put it into a realistic, social context that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time." And we've already talked to you about how many pages you have on the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS. And in the section on the SDA you talk at some length about the patriotic league, paramilitary formations and the Mujahedin. And in Dr. Nielsen's report, he has a section dealing with paramilitaries and the interaction between those groups and the RS MUP. My question is: Did you have information about the various Serb paramilitary groups operating in Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that I read Mr. Nielsen's report shows that I acquainted myself with these things in this manner too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P591.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have a tab number for this one. This is one of Dr. Nielsen's documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is General Tolimir's report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic. Professor, this is dated the 28th of July, 1992. Well, I said general but then he was Colonel Tolimir of the army security. Have you ever seen this document before? I can give you a hard copy if that's easier to look through the whole thing rather than turning page by page.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not a problem. I can look at it as it is. I don't think I have seen it before. I think not. However, in my original sources, I did have documents which addressed this subject, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel Tolimir talks about several alleged paramilitary groups throughout the territory. On this page, last paragraph of the English and for you it's the third paragraph, he is talking about the Serbian defence forces from Banja Luka. Could you have a read of that paragraph and tell us if you were aware of this information when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not anything that was called the Serbian defence forces, no. I was not aware at all that there was a formation with this name, the Serbian defence forces from Banja Luka. While writing my report I never came across such a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- but you were aware of the existence of a Special Police detachment in the Banja Luka CSB, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it is mentioned in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that one of the best ways to analyse the activities of these three main political parties was to resort to a broader set of material than, I guess, the materials you were furnished. How did you go about to finding that material? You told us about your private collection that you had, but did you start surfing the Internet or Googling? How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source materials which I used for my report was, in total, the result of all possible ways of collecting materials. Of course, I do not mean by theft of any kind, but by reading documents, monographs, borrowing books from friends if someone had a good book that might help me or not. So I knew that someone had a specific book, why wouldn't I ask him to borrow the book to me. I do this on a daily basis, so also for this report I used everything that I could get my hands on legally so as to get all the materials that might help me to produce the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it all available means does include Internet research; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you think that you can realistically pose any serious challenge to the witness's report through this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I actually do, Your Honour, because I think some of the sources that he has footnoted from the Internet, when you look at them you will see, I hope you will see, that there's some reason to believe that that might not be the best source to cite in a report of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As I suggested a while ago, I believe it would be more expeditious if you would go directly to the documents which you think that the witness should have used in his reports but failed or omitted to do, so as to, you know, bring yourself straight to the point that you want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I felt I first needed to establish that he actually had gotten the source in that fashion and not in some other way as handed to him by a friend or something from the Defence. I will come back to some of the specific sources when I get to the actual section of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I would like now to ask you about your comment concerning the section on the SDA and the Muslims. At page 20038, you said: "On the basis of certain documents I analysed, I got the impression that the party for democratic action, in particular, made an effort to exercise dominant influence especially in those ministries called the ministries of force." Are you saying, Professor, it was your conclusion that the SDA was trying harder than the SDS and/or the HDZ to exercise dominant influence in those ministries of force? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my expert report I specifically drew one such conclusion, especially having in mind the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH, and I tried to support that by documents in the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us which certain documents gave you that impression? Are those simply the ones listed in your footnotes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying once again I would like to be shown a paragraph from my report with a specific source and then we can discuss it, because I do not wish to try to remember. Can you please refer me to a paragraph in which I stated a certain conclusion then I will also tell you what was the source with which I would support that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I will come to that a little later, Professor. You also talked about the regional communities and the problems these cause for the functioning of the RS MUP in 1992. You talked about the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina. First of all, let's talk about the de jure versus de facto establishment of organs --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis. Just 68, 13, it's recorded "RS MUP," I believe you were referencing to MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. SR MUP maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'm referring to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because as I understand it, Professor, isn't part of your conclusions the conclusion that for the RS MUP in 1992, one of the contributing factors to the difficult situation in which it was working was the existence of these Serb autonomous regions, like the autonomous region of the Krajina which had, you say, established its own organs; am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the ways in which I analysed the functioning of the MUP, and I emphasised then, as well, that this particularly referred to the period until the end of September 1992. Though there were problems later on which were residual due to the existence of these autonomous regions, but certainly until the end of September, this had a significant impact on the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your report, you talk about the ARK and you make reference to other autonomous regions, but I don't think you name any. Can you tell us what other Serb autonomous regions were created or were functioning in and after April 1992? Can you name any besides the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never dealt with the number or exact names but I know that there was such a Serbian autonomous region around wider Sarajevo area, it was called Romanija something. I know that there was one in the area of Herzegovina as well, but I never dealt with them in the report in such a way that I would enumerate them and list their full names. It is a fact that they did exist and this fact by itself, and, in particular, the fact that there was the Autonomous Region of Krajina which prompted me to draw such a conclusion. Through further analysis on several occasions, I took several positions and finally I drew some conclusions about the problems which existed because of the existence of these autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to put to you, Professor, is that from the information that you had and referred to relating to the ARK, you try to extend that to other regions where I don't believe you have any support for the evidence that in those other Serb autonomous regions they had established their own organs. You mentioned something called Romanija, I think there, indeed, was a Serb autonomous region called Romanija Birac, does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe we may have seen a document or a reference to a Serb autonomous region for Northern Bosnia, and maybe one for Semberija Majevica. But did you see any documents showing that other than being an idea or being on paper, that they ever actually got set up and functioned and created organs of their own? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with this issue, particularly, but they are discussed in many documents, these Serbian autonomous regions, the documents which I've read, and references are partly made in these documents and sources that are of such nature that made me draw the conclusions I have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, I know it's early, but I have been fighting my allergies and my cough and my cold all week and I would like to request if we could recess 8 minutes early today and perhaps when we come back on Monday I can go more directly to some of the things Judge Harhoff has suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bajagic, we are about to take the adjournment for the weekend. I remind you of what I alerted you to at the adjournment on the first day that in such discussions as you have, you can't discuss your testimony until you are released. So I trust everyone has a safe weekend and we resume in this courtroom on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.38 p.m.
